questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: What is the primary goal of research ethics?
questions.rationale: The first and most important goal is to protect human participants, their dignity, rights and welfare.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Goals of research ethics (PDF p. 114)
questions.quote: The primary and most important goal is to protect and safeguard human participants

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: Which body reviews a study to make sure participants' rights and welfare are protected?
questions.rationale: The REC/IRB examines research to see that it respects participants' rights, dignity and welfare.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Research ethics (PDF p. 114)
questions.quote: The Research Ethics Committee (REC)/Institutional Review Board (IRB) examines the research

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: The Declaration of Helsinki (1964) states that in research, the subject's well-being should take precedence over:
questions.rationale: Helsinki: considerations of the subject's well-being take precedence over the interests of science and society.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Nuremberg Code and Helsinki (PDF p. 115)
questions.quote: considerations related to the well-being of the human subject should take precedence over the interests of science and socieO'

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which organization issued the Declaration of Helsinki?
questions.rationale: The World Medical Association adopted the Declaration of Helsinki in 1964, building on the Nuremberg principles.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Nuremberg Code and Helsinki (PDF p. 115)
questions.quote: The World Medical Association adopted and developed the Nuremberg principles in the Declaration of Helsinki in 1964

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: A researcher lies to participants about the study, though the goal is worthwhile. Under a duty-based approach this research is:
questions.rationale: In the duty-based approach, deceiving participants makes research unethical even if the goal is worthy.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Ethical approaches in research (PDF p. 116)
questions.quote: if the researcher lies to or dæeives the in any manrrr, the research would be considered unethical

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: A nurse researcher changes data so results look significant. This violates:
questions.rationale: Honesty requires reporting data and results truthfully; fabrication and falsification are prohibited.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Principles of research ethics (PDF p. 117)
questions.quote: Data fabrication, falsification, or misrepresentation are prohibited.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: A student copies paragraphs from a journal into her thesis without citing them. This is:
questions.rationale: Respect for intellectual property requires crediting others; plagiarism is never acceptable.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Principles of research ethics (PDF p. 118)
questions.quote: PlaØarism is never acceptable.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Keeping participants' names off all reports so no one can identify them protects:
questions.rationale: Anonymity means keeping the participant's identity hidden and not disclosing identifying details.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Principles of research ethics (PDF p. 118)
questions.quote: It entails keeping the participant's identity hidden.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: A participant holds out her arm for a blood pressure reading without saying anything. This is:
questions.rationale: Implied consent is inferred from behavior; express consent is an active oral or written assertion.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Informed consent (PDF p. 120)
questions.quote: Implied permission is based on an assumption inferted from behavior, such as the volunteering of an arm

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: Halfway through a study, the procedures change significantly. The researcher must:
questions.rationale: Consent is an ongoing process; if conditions or techniques change significantly, consent must be renewed.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Delivering information (PDF p. 121)
questions.quote: If the research's conditions or techniques change siY1ificantly, the consent must be renewed.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: A participant wants to leave a study midway. The researcher should:
questions.rationale: Participants may withdraw at any time, without giving a reason, penalty or loss of benefits.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Information for participants (PDF p. 123)
questions.quote: free to withdraw from the research at any time without having to give any reason, and without penalty

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Prisoners and patients who cannot consent need extra protection in research because they are:
questions.rationale: Vulnerability is a significant inability to protect one's own interests; vulnerable groups need special safeguards (CIOMS).
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Justice and vulnerability (PDF p. 121)
questions.quote: "Vulnerability" refers to a significant inability to safeguard one's own interests

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: A study needs to give a placebo without telling participants which group they are in. Before using deception, the researcher must:
questions.rationale: Deception must be approved by a Research Ethics Committee and defended by the main investigator.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Deception (PDF p. 122)
questions.quote: A Research Ethics Committee must approve this procedure before it can be utilized

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: A study's relevance to a current health problem is called its:
questions.rationale: Social value is the study's relevance to a current social or health problem; human participation is justified only by it.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Social value (PDF p. 122)
questions.quote: The social value of a study is defined as its relevance to a current social or health problem

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: In research, 'risk' combines the severity of possible harm with its:
questions.rationale: Risk has two dimensions: the size or severity of harm and the likelihood that it occurs.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Identifying risks (PDF p. 124)
questions.quote: (1) the size or severity of the possible harm, and (2) the possibility of that harm occurring

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Which research design is called the 'gold standard' because it reduces bias?
questions.rationale: The RCT reduces bias and controls confounding; cohort or case-control designs are used when an RCT is not ethical or feasible.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Identifying benefits (PDF p. 125)
questions.quote: the randomized controlled clinical trial (RCT) is sometimes referred to as the "gold standard" of research

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: Why can't researchers randomly assign non-smokers to start smoking to study harm?
questions.rationale: Ethical limits rule out such RCTs; cohort or case-control designs are used instead.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Identifying benefits (PDF p. 125)
questions.quote: could not ethically conduct a study in which non-smokers were invited to start smoking

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Some argue an underpowered study is unethical because:
questions.rationale: Studies with too small samples may lack statistical power, so they expose participants to risk with little value.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Identifying benefits (PDF p. 125)
questions.quote: Some argue that underpowered experiments are intrinsically unethical because they have no potential value.

questions.subject: NP III
questions.stem: Storing research data with codes kept separate from names is a way to:
questions.rationale: Ways to minimize risk include storing data so it cannot be linked to individuals and keeping key codes separate.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Ways to minimize risk (PDF p. 129)
questions.quote: limit access to key codes and store it separately from the data

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: An anonymous survey with no identifiers usually qualifies for which REC review level?
questions.rationale: Exempt review covers least-risk studies such as anonymous surveys; it still needs REC approval and registration.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Levels of REC review (PDF p. 130)
questions.quote: Despite the term "exempt," this type ofrescarch still requires REC/IRB approval and registration.

questions.subject: NP I
questions.stem: Collecting saliva samples with names attached is usually reviewed as:
questions.rationale: Minimal-risk studies collecting identified data or noninvasive specimens qualify for expedited review.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 4 Levels of REC review (PDF p. 130)
questions.quote: Collection Of biological specimens (e.g., hair, saliva) for research by noninvasive means

questions.subject: NP V
questions.stem: When family members disagree about an incompetent patient's care, the nurse's first responsibility is to:
questions.rationale: The nurse's primary responsibility is to the patient, advocating for her after understanding the conflict.
questions.source: Udan, Healthcare Ethics (2023), Ch. 3.2 Case: end-of-life care and role of nurses (PDF p. 111)
questions.quote: The nurse's first and foremost responsibility is towards the primary patient
